AI Model Misbehavior
OpenAI disclosed
six new cases
of concerning behavior by its AI models, including systems that hid mistakes, fabricated data, and took unauthorized actions. The company responded with a new framework for investigating and publicly reporting such incidents.
The incidents occurred during training or evaluation, not customer deployments, over the past six months. In one case, a model wrote hidden instructions reminding itself to conceal errors; another inserted "jailbreak-like" commands into its own notes. Under the new framework, employees can flag concerning behavior, which is routed into one of three investigation tracks. The move follows OpenAI's report on a July incident involving Hugging Face in which models circumvented safeguards and accessed third-party systems (see a database of
reported AI incidents
The announcement follows public calls for a slowdown in AI development: A
recent poll
found 63% of Americans believe advanced AI poses at least a moderate risk of eventually causing human extinction (watch how that

South Africa Slayings
South African police
confirmed the discovery
of a ninth female murder victim yesterday in a municipality east of Johannesburg. Authorities are investigating a possible link between the killings that occurred over the last two months.
The victims were found across several Ekurhuleni towns. All were in their 20s or 30s and partially or fully nude. A suspect linked to the first victim, found July 15, is in custody but has not been charged. Police are pursuing a person of interest but have not disclosed any specific case ties. The murders have ignited fear in South Africa, where
female homicide rates
are roughly six times the global average and 44% of femicide cases go unsolved.
Serial killing sprees in the US
have
dropped
over 85%
since peaking in the 1970s, from around 300 active killers to fewer than 50 in the 2010s. The trend is largely attributed to forensic science advancements, stricter parole policies, and changing public behavior—like the decline in hitchhiking.

Fiji's HIV Emergency
Fiji declared a
national HIV emergency
this week, finding one in 60 residents has the bloodborne virus, up from one in 167 five years ago.
The government partly attributes the spike to expanded testing efforts, with only 39% of infected individuals aware they are HIV positive. Experts say infections likely also began rising around 2019, as Fiji became a "superhighway" for drugs from Latin America and Asia to lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand (
watch documentary
). This has increased drug use in Fiji too, primarily among sex workers. More than half of the cases with known modes of transmission were traced to sex, while over 42% were tied to injecting drugs.
Only 22% of infected people are receiving treatment, compared with 78% globally. Fiji is working with Australia, New Zealand, India, and NGOs to provide free antiretrovirals, which studies show reduce HIV to undetectable levels in 90% of patients and lower the risk of AIDS. Watch how
